post-study-work-visa.title: France Post-Study Work Visa for Indian Students
paragraphs: France Post-Study Work Visa for Indian Students
Introduction

Completing your degree in France is a major achievement, but many international students have another important decision to make after graduation: should they return to India or stay in France and begin their professional career?

For Indian students, France offers a useful opportunity to make this transition. Eligible graduates can apply for a post-study residence permit that gives them time to look for employment or develop a business project related to their education. A special arrangement between India and France also allows qualifying Indian graduates to extend this period to up to two years.

There is another benefit that often creates confusion: eligible Indian alumni can apply for a multiple-entry visa with a validity of up to five years. However, this is a short-stay travel visa, not a work permit.
This guide explains the difference between these options, who can apply, how long you can stay, what work you are allowed to do and how to apply from France or India.
What Is France's Post-Study Work Visa?

France does not have a post-study work visa under the same name used in countries such as the UK. Instead, international graduates can apply for a residence permit known as Recherche d'emploi ou création d'entreprise (RECE), which translates to Job Search or Business Creation.

The permit is designed for eligible graduates who want to remain in France after completing higher education. It gives them time to find a suitable job or prepare a business project connected to their academic qualification.

Indian students may also benefit from the Autorisation Provisoire de Séjour (APS) arrangement under the India-France Migration and Mobility Partnership Agreement. This provides qualifying Indian graduates with an initial one-year stay, which can be extended by another year under the bilateral arrangement.
Key Features of the Post-Study Permit
Official name: Recherche d'emploi ou création d'entreprise (RECE).
Commonly used term: APS (Autorisation Provisoire de Séjour), particularly when discussing the special arrangement for Indian graduates.
Purpose: To search for employment or prepare a business project related to your education.
Job offer at the time of application: Not required.
Duration: Generally one year under the standard RECE route. Qualifying Indian graduates may be eligible for an additional year under the bilateral arrangement.
Application location: Eligible graduates can apply in France. Those who have returned to India may also have a separate application route within four years of graduation.

The RECE and APS terms are often used interchangeably in discussions about post-study options, but they are not identical legal routes. The exact permit and conditions depend on the graduate's nationality, qualification and place of application.
Who Is Eligible for the France Post-Study Work Visa?
Eligibility depends on the qualification you have completed, your nationality and whether you are applying from France or after returning to India.
Eligibility for Indian Students Applying in France
To qualify for the special post-study arrangement, Indian graduates generally need to meet the following conditions:
Nationality: You must be an Indian citizen.
Degree level: You must have completed a qualification at least equivalent to a Master's degree.
Institution: Your qualification must be from a French higher education institution authorised or recognised under the applicable rules.
Immigration status: You should hold a valid student residence permit or student mobility residence status when applying in France.
Graduation period: For the standard RECE application made in France, the qualifying degree must generally have been obtained within the previous 12 months.

The India-France agreement also refers to certain Indian higher education institutions linked with French institutions through an international diploma-awarding partnership. Students in such programmes should confirm whether their qualification meets the agreement's requirements.
Does a Bachelor's Degree Qualify?
Not every Bachelor's degree automatically makes a student eligible for the two-year Indian post-study arrangement.

A professional Bachelor's degree, such as a Licence Professionnelle, may qualify under France's standard RECE rules. However, the special two-year arrangement for Indian graduates is based on completing a qualification at least equivalent to a Master's degree.
A regular three-year Bachelor's degree or a short certificate should not be assumed to qualify for this route.

How Long Can You Stay in France After Graduation?
The length of your post-study stay depends on the permit you apply for and whether you qualify under the India-France agreement.
1. Indian Master's and PhD Graduates
Indian graduates with a qualifying Master's-level or higher degree may benefit from the bilateral arrangement.
Initial stay: 12 months.
Possible extension: Another 12 months.
Maximum potential duration: 24 months.
The extension is subject to the applicable procedure and approval. Students should not assume that the second year is granted automatically.
2. Standard RECE Applicants
Under the general RECE route, the job-search or business-creation residence permit is valid for one year and is not renewable under the standard rules.
This is why Indian graduates should check whether they qualify for the separate APS arrangement rather than relying only on the general RECE process.
3. Indian Graduates Applying from India
If you complete a qualifying Master's-level degree in France and return to India, you may still be able to apply for a Job Search / Business Creation long-stay visa.
The application must generally be made within four years of graduation. This route is intended for graduates who have left France and want to return to look for employment or establish a business.

The VLS-TS issued through this route is generally valid for one year and is not renewable under the standard procedure. It should not be confused with the one-year-plus-one-year APS arrangement available to eligible Indian graduates applying under the bilateral route in France.
The Five-Year Alumni Visa: A Special Benefit for Indian Graduates

One of the most discussed benefits for Indian alumni is the five-year validity visa. It was introduced to make travel between India and France easier and to strengthen academic, professional and cultural connections between the two countries.
However, it is important to understand what this visa actually allows.
The five-year alumni visa is a multiple-entry short-stay visa, not a post-study work visa.
Who Can Apply?
Indian nationals may be eligible if they:
Hold a Master's degree or a higher qualification.
Have completed at least one semester of study in France during their university education.
Can provide evidence of their academic stay in France.
Apply through the appropriate French visa application process in India.

The Master's degree does not necessarily have to be obtained in France. The key requirement is that the applicant must have reached Master's level and completed at least one qualifying semester of study in France.
What Does the Five-Year Visa Allow?
Multiple entries into France during the visa's validity.
Short visits for tourism, private purposes and eligible business activities.
Visits of up to 90 days within any 180-day period in the Schengen Area.
Easier travel between India and France for eligible alumni.
The visa may be issued with a validity of up to five years, depending on the passport's validity and the consulate's decision.
What Does It Not Allow?
Full-time employment in France.
Taking up a job as a regular employee.
Using the visa as a substitute for a job-search residence permit.
Staying continuously in France for five years.
If your goal is to find employment and begin working in France, you need the appropriate long-stay job-search permit or work residence permit.

Work Rights Under the France Post-Study Permit
The RECE or APS permit gives eligible graduates an opportunity to move towards professional employment without first securing a long-term work residence permit.
However, this does not mean that every type of job or employment arrangement is automatically allowed.
1. Employment Related to Your Studies
Graduates can take up salaried employment related to their academic training or research, subject to the applicable salary requirement.
Under the French administration's published RECE rules, the job must:
Be related to the graduate's studies or research.
Provide gross monthly remuneration above €2,800.53 under the threshold published in June 2026.
When these conditions are met, the employer is exempt from applying for a separate work authorisation under this route.
2. Working Hours

The 964-hour annual limit generally applies to international students working under student residence status. It should not be presented as a universal part-time work allowance under the post-study RECE permit.
The employment conditions change once a graduate moves from student status to a post-study residence permit. Students should check the rights attached to their actual permit before accepting work.
3. Starting a Business
The permit also provides an opportunity to prepare a business creation project.

The proposed business should be connected to the graduate's education or professional training. Applicants may need to provide evidence explaining the nature of the project and how it relates to their qualification.
A separate residence status may be required once the business is established and the graduate moves into a longer-term professional activity.
4. Changing Employers

The job-search permit is not tied to one specific employer. If you find another qualifying opportunity, you can explore a change in employment while complying with the conditions of your residence permit.
However, you must maintain valid immigration status and apply for the appropriate change of status before your current permit expires.
Switching from a Post-Study Permit to a Work Visa
The post-study permit is a temporary arrangement. Once you secure suitable employment or establish a qualifying business, you can apply to change your residence status.
The right option depends on your salary, qualification, employment contract and professional role.
1. Salarié Residence Permit
The Salarié route is generally used by foreign graduates who secure qualifying salaried employment in France.

For graduates applying through the RECE route, the job must meet the relevant connection-to-studies and salary conditions. The French administration's June 2026 published threshold for this route is more than €2,800.53 gross per month.
The employer and employee must complete the applicable change-of-status and work-related formalities.
2. Talent Residence Permit for Qualified Employees
The Talent residence permit, commonly still called the Passeport Talent, is another option for highly qualified professionals.
One relevant category is the Talent – Qualified Employee route.
Under the rules published in June 2026:
The minimum annual gross salary threshold is €39,582.
The applicant must meet the qualification and employment conditions for the category.
The permit can provide a longer residence period than the standard employee route.
The Talent route is not automatically available to every Master's graduate. A qualifying job offer and the relevant professional and academic conditions are required.
3. European Blue Card
Highly qualified professionals may also explore the EU Blue Card route.
This category has a higher salary requirement and additional qualification or professional experience conditions. The published annual gross salary threshold in June 2026 was €59,373.
It can be a suitable option for eligible professionals who secure higher-paying employment in France.

How to Apply for the France Post-Study Work Visa
The application process depends on whether you are still living in France after graduation or have already returned to India.
If You Are Applying from France
Most graduates apply before their student residence permit expires.
Step 1: Complete Your Degree
You should obtain your final degree certificate or an official certificate of successful completion, known as an attestation de réussite.
Step 2: Check Your Eligibility

Confirm that your qualification meets the Master's-level or other applicable requirements. Indian graduates should also check whether they qualify for the APS arrangement under the bilateral agreement.
Step 3: Contact Your Local Prefecture
Applications made from within France are handled by the prefecture or sub-prefecture responsible for your place of residence. The procedure may differ depending on your location.
Step 4: Submit Your Application
For the standard RECE route, the application should generally be submitted during the two months before the expiry of your student residence card or student mobility status.
Follow the instructions of your local prefecture and submit the required documents through the specified online or administrative process.
Step 5: Receive the Application Receipt
If your application is complete, the prefecture may issue a temporary receipt while your application is being examined. Keep this document and check the work and travel rights it provides.
Step 6: Collect Your Residence Permit
Once the application is approved, follow the prefecture's instructions for paying the applicable charges and collecting your residence card.
If You Have Already Returned to India
Indian graduates who have left France after completing a qualifying Master's-level degree may apply for the Job Search / Business Creation long-stay visa within four years of graduation.
Step 1: Check the Four-Year Eligibility Window
Make sure your French qualification and graduation date meet the requirements. The four-year period is calculated from the date of graduation.
Step 2: Start an Application on France-Visas
Complete the relevant online application for the Job Search / Business Creation long-stay visa.
Step 3: Prepare Your Documents
Collect your degree certificate, proof of your previous student residence status in France and other supporting documents required by the visa process.
Step 4: Book a VFS Appointment
Book an appointment at the appropriate French visa application centre in India. Submit your application and biometrics as instructed.
Step 5: Wait for the Decision
The French consular authorities assess the application. Processing times can vary, so apply well before your intended travel date.
Step 6: Travel to France and Validate Your Visa
If your VLS-TS is approved, travel to France and complete the online validation process within three months of arrival. Pay the applicable validation tax as instructed.
Documents Required for the France Post-Study Work Visa
The exact document list depends on whether you are applying in France or India. However, the following documents are commonly relevant.
For Applications Made in France
Valid passport.
Current student residence card or valid student VLS-TS.
Master's degree or equivalent qualification.
Attestation de réussite, if the final degree certificate has not yet been issued.
Proof of residential address in France.
Recent passport-size photographs.
Proof of health insurance.
Supporting documents for a proposed business project, if applicable.
Any additional declaration or document requested by the prefecture.
For Applications Made from India
Valid passport.
Copy of the Master's degree or equivalent qualification obtained in France.
Copy of the previous student residence permit or VLS-TS.
Evidence of the academic stay in France.
Supporting documents requested through the France-Visas application process.
Proof of the proposed business project, where applicable.
Any additional documents requested by the French consulate.
The French authorities may ask for additional documents depending on the applicant's circumstances. Always follow the personalised checklist generated for your application.
Fees and Financial Planning
Applying for a post-study residence permit involves administrative charges. The amount depends on the application route and the type of document issued.

These are the charges published for the relevant routes in the French administration's June 2026 information. They should be checked again before submitting an application because fees can change.
Planning Your Living Expenses
A post-study permit gives you time to look for work, but it does not guarantee employment or provide a monthly living allowance.
Before applying, plan for expenses such as:
Rent and accommodation deposits.
Food and groceries.
Local transportation.
Health insurance and medical expenses.
Mobile and internet services.
Visa and residence permit charges.
Emergency savings while searching for employment.

If you are applying from India, check the financial evidence required by the consulate. If you are already in France, make sure you have enough savings to support yourself during the job-search period.
Common Myths About the France Post-Study Work Visa
There is a lot of confusion around the RECE, APS and five-year alumni visa. Understanding the actual rules can help students avoid costly mistakes.
Myth 1: "Indian students get a five-year post-study work visa."

Reality: The five-year alumni visa is a multiple-entry short-stay visa. It allows eligible Indian alumni to visit France, but it does not provide permission to work or look for a job. The post-study job-search route is separate.
Myth 2: "Every international student can stay for two years after graduation."

Reality: The two-year arrangement is linked to the India-France agreement and applies to qualifying Indian graduates with a Master's-level or higher qualification. Other international graduates generally follow the standard RECE rules.
Myth 3: "A regular Bachelor's degree is enough to qualify."

Reality: The main post-study route requires a qualifying professional degree or a qualification at least equivalent to a Master's, depending on the category. A standard Bachelor's degree should not be assumed to qualify for the Indian two-year arrangement.
Myth 4: "The RECE permit allows me to work in any job without restrictions."

Reality: Employment under the relevant job-search route must meet the applicable conditions, including a connection to your studies and the prescribed salary threshold. The 964-hour student work limit should not be confused with post-study employment rules.
Myth 5: "I must remain in France after graduation to use the job-search route."
Reality: Eligible graduates who have returned to India may apply for a Job Search / Business Creation long-stay visa within four years of completing a qualifying Master's-level degree in France.
Myth 6: "Getting the post-study permit guarantees permanent residency."

Reality: The RECE or APS is a temporary residence arrangement. Graduates generally need to move to an appropriate long-term work or business residence status if they want to continue living and working in France. Permanent or long-term residence is a separate application with its own conditions.
Pros and Cons of Staying in France After Graduation
The post-study route gives Indian graduates additional time to explore professional opportunities, but it is important to consider both its advantages and limitations.
Advantages
No job offer required at the start: Eligible graduates can apply for the job-search permit before securing employment.
Additional time to find work: Qualifying Indian graduates may have up to two years under the bilateral arrangement.
Opportunity to build a career: Graduates can explore professional opportunities connected to their education.
Business creation option: The permit can also support the preparation of a relevant business project.
Option to apply after returning to India: Eligible graduates may use the separate four-year application window to return to France for job searching.
Five-year alumni travel benefit: Eligible Indian alumni can apply for a separate multiple-entry short-stay visa.
Limitations
No guaranteed employment: The permit provides time to search, not a job placement.
Specific employment conditions: A qualifying job must meet the relevant academic connection and salary requirements.
Limited validity: The post-study permit is temporary and cannot be treated as a permanent residence route.
Living expenses continue: Graduates must arrange their own funds while looking for employment.
French language can matter: Many employers require French proficiency, particularly for customer-facing and locally regulated roles.
A separate status is required for long-term work: Graduates need to apply for the appropriate work or business residence permit to continue their stay.
Tips for Finding a Job in France After Graduation
Getting the right residence permit is only one part of building a career in France. Students should begin preparing for employment well before their final semester.
Start applying before graduation: Research companies and internship opportunities while you are still studying.
Prepare a French-style CV: Keep your CV clear, relevant and focused on your qualifications and professional experience.
Improve your French language skills: English-speaking roles are available, but French proficiency can expand your employment opportunities.
Use university career services: Attend career fairs, recruitment events and employer networking sessions.
Build a professional network: Connect with alumni, recruiters and professionals working in your chosen industry.
Research salary requirements: Understand the salary conditions attached to your intended residence permit before accepting an offer.
Keep your documents ready: Maintain copies of your degree, transcripts, residence documents and employment records.
Plan your change of status early: Do not wait until the final weeks of your post-study permit to begin the next application.
Frequently Asked Questions About the France Post-Study Work Visa
1. Can Indian students stay in France after completing their Master's degree?

Yes. Eligible Indian graduates with a Master's-level or higher qualification can apply for a post-study residence arrangement. Under the India-France agreement, the stay may be extended from an initial 12 months to a maximum of 24 months, subject to the applicable conditions and approval.
2. Is the France post-study work visa valid for five years?
No. The post-study job-search permit is separate from the five-year alumni visa. The latter is a multiple-entry short-stay visa and does not allow employment or job searching.
3. Can I apply for the France job-search visa after returning to India?
Yes. Graduates who have completed a qualifying Master's-level degree in France and have left the country may apply for a Job Search / Business Creation long-stay visa within four years of graduation.
4. Can I work full-time on the RECE or APS permit?

Qualifying salaried employment is permitted when the job meets the relevant conditions, including a connection to your studies and the applicable salary threshold. The French administration's published June 2026 threshold is more than €2,800.53 gross per month for the relevant RECE employment route.
5. Can I work in any field while searching for a job?

You should not assume that the permit allows unrestricted employment in any field. The qualifying employment route requires a job related to your academic training or research and compliance with the applicable salary conditions.
6. Can I start a business in France after graduation?

Yes. The job-search/business-creation route also allows eligible graduates to prepare a business project related to their education. You may need to change to a suitable business residence permit once you begin operating the business.
7. Is the five-year alumni visa available to all Indian students?

No. Applicants must meet the relevant conditions, including holding a Master's degree or higher qualification and having completed at least one semester of study in France. They must also apply through the appropriate process in India.
8. Does the five-year alumni visa allow me to work in France?
No. It is a short-stay visa for visits and does not authorise employment or job searching. A separate work or residence permit is required for professional activity.
9. Can I get permanent residency after the post-study permit?

The post-study permit does not automatically grant permanent or long-term residence. You generally need to qualify for another residence category and meet the applicable residence, employment and other legal conditions.
10. Do I need IELTS or French language certification to apply?

There is no universal IELTS or French-language test requirement for the post-study residence permit itself. However, employers may require language proficiency, and certain regulated professions have additional requirements.
Start Planning Your Career in France

France offers Indian graduates more than one way to remain connected with the country after completing higher education. The post-study RECE or APS route can provide valuable time to find employment or prepare a business project, while the separate five-year alumni visa makes short visits easier for eligible graduates.

The most important step is to understand which route applies to your qualification and circumstances. Check your eligibility early, prepare your documents and begin exploring career opportunities before graduation. With the right planning, your time in France can become the starting point for a professional career rather than the end of your academic journey.

scholarships.title: Scholarships in France for Indian Students
paragraphs: Scholarships in France for Indian Students

France offers several scholarship opportunities for international students, including Indian students planning to pursue undergraduate, postgraduate and doctoral studies. These scholarships are provided by the French government, universities, international organisations, private foundations and Indian funding bodies.

Depending on the programme, financial support may cover tuition fees, monthly living expenses, travel costs, health insurance or other study-related expenses. Some scholarships provide a fixed monthly allowance, while others reduce the tuition fee charged by a university.

For Indian students planning to study in France, it is important to understand that not every scholarship covers the full cost of education. The benefits, eligibility requirements and application procedures differ from one programme to another. Applying to the right scholarship based on your course, academic background and financial requirements can improve your chances of receiving support.
Why Apply for Scholarships in France?

Studying in France can involve expenses such as tuition fees, accommodation, food, transportation, health insurance and other personal costs. Scholarships can reduce this financial burden and make higher education in France more accessible.
Here are some reasons why Indian students should explore scholarship opportunities:
Lower education costs: Tuition fee scholarships and fee waivers can reduce the amount students need to pay to their university.
Support with living expenses: Selected scholarships provide monthly allowances to help students manage accommodation, food and daily expenses.
International academic exposure: Students get the opportunity to study at recognised French universities and interact with an international academic community.
Research opportunities: Several funding programmes support students pursuing doctoral studies and research projects in France.
Additional student benefits: Depending on the scholarship, students may receive health insurance, travel support, visa fee exemptions or accommodation assistance.
Types of Scholarships in France for Indian Students
Scholarships in France can be divided into different categories according to the organisation providing the funding.
1. French Government Scholarships

These scholarships are funded or supported by the French government and are available to eligible international students. Some programmes are specifically designed for Indian applicants, while others accept applications from students across the world.
Examples include:
France Excellence Eiffel Scholarship
France Excellence Charpak Scholarship
Other French government and embassy-supported scholarship programmes
2. University Scholarships in France

Many French universities and business schools provide scholarships to attract talented international students. These awards may be based on academic performance, financial need, leadership experience or the requirements of a particular programme.
Examples include the Émile Boutmy Scholarship at Sciences Po, the HEC Foundation Excellence Scholarship and the Université Paris-Saclay International Master's Scholarship.
3. International Scholarships
International funding programmes support students who want to study across multiple European countries or at institutions in different countries.
The Erasmus Mundus Joint Master's scholarship is one such opportunity. It allows selected students to pursue a joint master's programme offered by a group of European universities.
4. Indian Government and Private Scholarships

Indian students can also explore funding opportunities offered by the Government of India, charitable foundations and private organisations. These scholarships may support students pursuing higher education abroad, including in France, provided they meet the relevant conditions.
Examples include the National Overseas Scholarship, Inlaks Scholarship and other postgraduate funding programmes.
Top Scholarships in France for Indian Students

The following scholarships are worth exploring if you are planning to study in France. Their funding amounts and eligibility conditions vary, so students should always check the official scholarship rules before applying.
1. France Excellence Eiffel Scholarship

The France Excellence Eiffel Scholarship is one of the major French government scholarship programmes for international students. It is designed to help French higher education institutions attract talented students to master's and doctoral programmes.
The scholarship is intended for students with strong academic records and the potential to contribute to their professional fields after completing their education.
Key benefits:
Master's scholarship holders receive a monthly allowance of €1,200 under the rules applicable from January 2026.
Doctoral scholarship holders receive a monthly allowance of €2,000.
Additional services may include international and national transportation, insurance, assistance with accommodation searches and cultural activities.
The scholarship does not directly cover tuition fees.
Eligibility and important conditions:
It is available for master's and doctoral-level studies in specified fields.
Master's applicants must generally be 29 years old or younger, while doctoral applicants must generally be 35 years old or younger, subject to the programme regulations.
Applicants are assessed on academic merit and the selection priorities of the programme.
Students cannot submit an Eiffel application independently. A French higher education institution must select and nominate the candidate and submit the application.
2027 application information:
The 2027 campaign opened in October 2026. The deadline for French institutions to submit applications to Campus France is 6 January 2027. Results are scheduled to be announced from 12 April 2027.
Students interested in this scholarship should contact their preferred French university well before the national deadline because individual institutions may set earlier internal deadlines.
2. France Excellence Charpak Scholarship

The France Excellence Charpak Scholarship is a French government scholarship programme managed in India by the Embassy of France. It is designed to support Indian students who want to pursue higher education or academic activities in France.
The programme has different categories, including Bachelor's, Master's, Summer Training and Exchange scholarships. Each category has its own eligibility requirements and application process.
France Excellence Charpak Master's Scholarship
This category supports Indian students admitted to full-time master's programmes in France across different academic fields.
Key benefits:
A monthly living allowance of €860.
Exemption from visa fees for eligible applicants applying from India.
Exemption from Campus France procedure fees.
Student social security and additional health insurance.
Assistance in finding affordable accommodation, including priority access to CROUS residences where available.
Access to university meals at the reduced price of €1 and certain cultural activities.
Eligibility:
Applicants must be Indian citizens or hold an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card.
Applicants must be 30 years old or younger at the time of application.
They must be enrolled in or have completed studies at an Indian higher education institution, subject to the programme's detailed rules.
The course must be a full-time master's programme in France.
French language knowledge is an advantage but is not compulsory.

Important: The Charpak Master's Scholarship does not cover travel expenses from India to France or every expense related to a student's stay. Students should arrange additional funds for costs not covered by the award.
3. Erasmus Mundus Joint Master's Scholarship

The Erasmus Mundus Joint Master's scholarship is funded through the European Union's Erasmus+ programme. It supports outstanding students from around the world who want to pursue an international master's degree.

These programmes are jointly delivered by a group of higher education institutions. Students usually study in more than one country during the programme, and some participating universities are based in France.
Key benefits:
Scholarships can cover programme participation costs, including tuition-related costs.
Financial support contributes towards travel and visa expenses.
Selected students receive a living allowance.
Students gain academic experience at multiple international institutions.
Depending on the programme, graduates receive a joint degree or multiple degrees.
Eligibility and application:
Applicants must meet the academic and language requirements of the selected master's programme.
A relevant bachelor's degree or an equivalent qualification is generally required.
Students apply directly to the Erasmus Mundus programme or consortium, not through a general scholarship application.
Each programme sets its own admission requirements and application deadlines.
Applications for programmes starting in the following academic year commonly take place between October and January. However, the exact dates depend on the individual course.
4. Émile Boutmy Scholarship at Sciences Po
The Émile Boutmy Scholarship is offered by Sciences Po, a well-known French institution specialising in social sciences, international affairs, politics, economics and related subjects.
It is intended for talented international students from outside the European Union who are applying for eligible undergraduate or master's programmes.
Key benefits:
Undergraduate students may receive a full tuition fee exemption or a tuition reduction of €9,500.
Master's students may receive a tuition fee exemption of €18,500 per year for each of the two years of the programme.
The scholarship can significantly reduce the cost of studying at Sciences Po.
Eligibility:
Applicants must be first-time candidates to Sciences Po.
They must be citizens of a country outside the European Union.
Their household must not file taxes within the European Union.
They must apply for an eligible undergraduate or master's programme.
Selection is based on academic merit and the candidate's profile.
How to apply:

Students must indicate their interest in the Émile Boutmy Scholarship in the financial information section of their Sciences Po admission application. It is not a separate application that can be submitted after admission.
The scholarship has specific programme exclusions and application deadlines. Students should check the relevant admission cycle before applying.
5. HEC Foundation Excellence Scholarship
HEC Paris offers the HEC Foundation Excellence Scholarship to support talented students admitted to its eligible programmes.
The scholarship is intended for candidates with a non-French bachelor's or master's degree who demonstrate a strong academic profile.
Key benefits:
Selected students may receive financial support of up to €15,000.
The scholarship can help reduce the overall tuition cost.
Eligible admitted students are considered automatically, without a separate scholarship application.
Eligibility:
Applicants must hold a non-French bachelor's or master's degree.
They must be admitted to an eligible HEC Paris programme.
Scholarship decisions are based on the institution's selection process.
Students should check the latest HEC Paris scholarship information because eligibility and funding arrangements can differ between programmes.
6. Université Paris-Saclay International Master's Scholarship
Université Paris-Saclay provides an International Master's Scholarship to attract talented international students to its master's programmes.
The scholarship is aimed at international students with strong academic backgrounds who wish to study at the university.
Key benefits:
Financial support of €10,000 per academic year.
Additional travel and visa support of up to €900, depending on the applicant's country of origin.
The scholarship is paid monthly during the academic year, generally from September to June.
Students admitted to the first year of a master's programme may be considered for renewal in the second year, subject to academic progress and programme conditions.
Eligibility and conditions:
Both first-year and second-year master's students may be eligible.
Applicants must meet the university's admission and scholarship selection requirements.
Certain vocational programmes are excluded.
Students receiving other funding above the programme's permitted limit may be ineligible.
The scholarship cannot be combined with certain other awards, including Eiffel and Erasmus Mundus funding.
Students should check the university's current scholarship call to confirm whether applications are open for their intended intake.
Scholarships from India for Studying in France
Apart from French and European funding, Indian students can also explore scholarships and financial assistance offered by Indian government departments and private foundations.
1. National Overseas Scholarship (NOS)

The National Overseas Scholarship is a Government of India scheme that provides financial assistance to eligible students from specified disadvantaged communities who wish to pursue higher education abroad.

It supports master's and PhD-level studies at eligible foreign universities. Students planning to study in France may explore this scheme if their course and institution meet the applicable requirements.
Who can apply?
The scheme is intended for eligible candidates belonging to the following categories:
Scheduled Castes (SC).
De-notified, Nomadic and Semi-Nomadic Tribes.
Landless Agricultural Labourers.
Traditional Artisans.

The scheme has additional conditions relating to age, family income, academic performance, admission and the ranking or recognition of the foreign institution. For the 2026–27 guidelines, applicants should check the prescribed income and age limits before applying.

Important: The National Overseas Scholarship is not open to every Indian student. It is a category-specific scheme, and it supports master's and doctoral studies rather than general undergraduate study.
2. Inlaks Scholarship

The Inlaks Scholarship is offered by the Inlaks Shivdasani Foundation to support talented Indian graduates pursuing postgraduate education at selected institutions in the United States, the United Kingdom and Europe.
Students planning to study in France may explore this scholarship if their chosen institution, course and academic profile meet the foundation's requirements.
Key benefits:
Funding of up to US$120,000 under the 2027 scholarship information.
Support towards eligible tuition fees and other approved study-related expenses.
Opportunity to pursue postgraduate education at recognised international institutions.
Eligibility and important conditions:
Applicants must meet the foundation's nationality, residence and academic requirements.
They must secure admission to an eligible postgraduate programme and institution.

Certain subjects are excluded, including Business and Finance, Computer Science, most Engineering programmes, Fashion Design, Hospitality and Tourism, MBA or Management Studies, Medicine and related fields.
Specific exceptions apply to certain courses and institutions.

For the 2027 application cycle, the stated deadline is 31 March 2027 at 12 noon. Applicants should read the official instructions carefully because the list of eligible subjects and other conditions is detailed.
3. Narotam Sekhsaria Scholarship Programme
The Narotam Sekhsaria Scholarship Programme supports meritorious Indian students pursuing postgraduate studies at recognised institutions in India and abroad.
It is a useful funding option to explore for students planning postgraduate education in France, particularly those who require financial assistance beyond university scholarships.

The programme provides an interest-free loan scholarship, rather than a conventional grant that students can automatically treat as free funding. Applicants should check the current application cycle, eligible courses, repayment conditions and selection requirements before applying.

Eligibility Criteria for Scholarships in France

Each scholarship has its own eligibility requirements. However, most scholarship providers consider a combination of academic performance, admission status, nationality, financial background and the relevance of the selected course.
Before applying for scholarships in France, Indian students should review the following requirements.
1. Academic Performance

A strong academic record is important for merit-based scholarships. Universities and scholarship providers may consider previous examination results, grades, class rank, research work and academic achievements.
2. Admission to a French Institution

Many scholarships require students to have an admission offer from a recognised French university or an eligible programme. Some scholarships, such as Eiffel, require the institution to nominate the candidate.
3. Nationality and Age
Certain scholarships are available only to applicants from specific countries or age groups. For example, the Charpak Master's Scholarship has nationality and age conditions for Indian applicants.
4. Language Requirements

Students may need to demonstrate proficiency in English or French depending on the course. English-taught programmes may require IELTS, TOEFL or another accepted qualification, while French-taught programmes may require proof of French language proficiency.
5. Financial Background

Need-based scholarships may consider family income, financial documents and the student's ability to fund their education. Some awards are based primarily on academic merit rather than financial need.
6. Course and Subject Requirements
Some scholarships are restricted to particular academic fields or levels of study. Applicants should check whether their chosen programme is covered before preparing an application.
Documents Required for Scholarship Applications
Scholarship applications generally require academic, personal and financial documents. The exact list depends on the scholarship provider.
Students applying for scholarships in France may need the following:
Valid passport.
Updated academic transcripts and mark sheets.
Degree certificates or provisional certificates.
Curriculum Vitae (CV).
Statement of Purpose (SOP) or motivation letter.
Letters of recommendation.
Admission offer or proof of application to a French institution.
English or French language test scores, where required.
Research proposal for relevant doctoral or research scholarships.
Family income certificate or financial documents for need-based funding.
Portfolio or evidence of achievements, where required by the programme.
Applicants should prepare clear and accurate documents before the application deadline. Documents that are incomplete, inconsistent or submitted in an incorrect format may affect the application.
How to Apply for Scholarships in France from India

Applying for a scholarship requires planning because some programmes have separate admission and funding procedures. Students should identify suitable scholarships before or while applying to French universities.
Step 1: Choose Your Course and Study Level
Start by deciding whether you want to pursue a Bachelor's, Master's or PhD programme in France. Your course and academic level will determine which scholarships you can apply for.
Step 2: Shortlist French Universities
Research French universities and institutions offering your chosen course. Check their admission requirements, tuition fees, language requirements and available funding options.
Step 3: Find Suitable Scholarships

Explore French government scholarships, university funding, European programmes and Indian funding opportunities. Use the official scholarship websites and the Campus Bourses directory to identify awards based on your nationality, subject and study level.
Step 4: Check Eligibility and Deadlines

Read the scholarship guidelines carefully. Check age limits, academic requirements, eligible courses, funding coverage and application deadlines. Remember that some universities set internal deadlines earlier than the final scholarship deadline.
Step 5: Prepare Your Documents

Arrange your transcripts, CV, motivation letter, recommendation letters, admission documents and financial records. Follow the exact format and submission instructions provided by the scholarship authority.
Step 6: Submit Your Application

Apply through the correct channel. Some scholarships require a direct application, while others are submitted through the university or a scholarship consortium. For example, students cannot directly submit an Eiffel Scholarship application to Campus France.
Step 7: Track Your Application
Check your email and application portal regularly for updates, interview invitations, requests for additional documents and final results.
When Should Indian Students Apply for Scholarships in France?

Scholarship applications often open several months before the academic year begins. Students should start researching funding options while preparing their university applications rather than waiting until they receive an admission offer.
A practical approach is to:
12–15 months before the intake: Research courses, universities and scholarship opportunities.
9–12 months before the intake: Prepare for language tests, collect academic documents and begin university applications.
6–9 months before the intake: Submit scholarship applications according to individual deadlines.
3–6 months before the intake: Track scholarship results, arrange remaining finances and complete visa-related preparations.
These are planning guidelines, not fixed deadlines. Each scholarship follows its own calendar, and some application windows may be much earlier.
Tips to Improve Your Chances of Getting a Scholarship in France
Scholarships can be competitive, especially those offering substantial financial support. A well-prepared application can help demonstrate why you are a suitable candidate.
Maintain a strong academic record: Good grades and relevant academic achievements can strengthen a merit-based application.
Choose a suitable programme: Your selected course should match your previous education, interests and future career plans.
Write a clear motivation letter: Explain why you want to study in France, why you selected the institution and how the course supports your goals.
Highlight relevant experience: Internships, research projects, volunteering, leadership roles and extracurricular activities can add value to your application.
Apply before the deadline: Start early, especially when the university must nominate you for a scholarship.
Check the funding conditions: Understand what the scholarship covers and arrange additional funding if necessary.
Apply to more than one suitable opportunity: Where the rules permit, exploring multiple scholarships can improve your overall funding options.
Common Mistakes to Avoid When Applying for Scholarships
Students sometimes miss scholarship opportunities because they overlook basic application requirements. Keep the following points in mind:
Applying without checking eligibility: Do not spend time on scholarships for which you do not meet the nationality, age, course or academic requirements.
Missing university nomination deadlines: Some scholarships have an earlier internal deadline than the official closing date.
Submitting a generic motivation letter: Your application should explain why you are suitable for that particular scholarship and course.
Assuming every scholarship is fully funded: Some awards cover only tuition fees or provide a limited living allowance.
Ignoring excluded subjects: Certain funding programmes do not support specific courses or professional degrees.
Relying on outdated information: Scholarship amounts, application dates and eligibility rules can change every year.
Frequently Asked Questions About Scholarships in France
1. Can Indian students get scholarships to study in France?

Yes. Indian students can apply for several scholarships offered by the French government, French universities, European funding programmes and Indian organisations. Eligibility depends on the scholarship and the selected course.
2. Which are the best scholarships in France for Indian students?

Some important options include the France Excellence Eiffel Scholarship, France Excellence Charpak Scholarship, Erasmus Mundus Joint Master's Scholarship, Émile Boutmy Scholarship, HEC Foundation Excellence Scholarship and Université Paris-Saclay International Master's Scholarship.
3. Are there fully funded scholarships in France for Indian students?

Yes. Some scholarships provide substantial financial support towards tuition, living expenses, travel or other costs. However, the term "fully funded" should be checked against the actual benefits and exclusions of each programme. Not every scholarship covers every expense.
4. Can I study in France with a 100% scholarship?

It is possible to receive a full tuition fee exemption through certain university scholarships. Some international scholarships also contribute towards living and travel expenses. However, receiving a scholarship that covers all education and personal expenses is competitive and depends on the programme.
5. Is IELTS compulsory for scholarships in France?

IELTS is not compulsory for every scholarship. Language requirements depend on the university and course. English-taught programmes may accept IELTS, TOEFL or other proof of English proficiency, while French-taught programmes may require French language certification.
6. Can I apply for the Eiffel Scholarship directly?

No. Students cannot submit an Eiffel Scholarship application independently. They must contact a French higher education institution, and the institution must select and submit the application on their behalf.
7. Does the Charpak Scholarship cover all expenses?

No. The Charpak Master's Scholarship provides a monthly allowance and specified benefits such as social security, additional health insurance and visa fee exemption for eligible applicants applying from India. It does not cover travel from India to France or every expense related to the student's stay.
8. Can I apply for more than one scholarship in France?

Students can explore multiple scholarship opportunities, but they must check the rules of each programme. Some scholarships cannot be combined with other funding, while others may allow additional financial support.
9. When should I start applying for scholarships in France?

It is advisable to start researching scholarships around 9–12 months before your intended intake. Some programmes require university nomination or have early deadlines, so students should begin even earlier when necessary.
10. Where can I find scholarships for studying in France?

Students can check the official websites of Campus France, French universities, Erasmus Mundus programmes, the Embassy of France in India and relevant Indian scholarship organisations. Campus Bourses is also a useful directory for finding funding based on nationality, academic field and study level.
Plan Your Studies in France with the Right Funding

Finding the right scholarship is an important part of planning your education in France. The best option depends on your academic background, chosen course, university, eligibility and financial requirements.

Indian students should compare the available scholarships carefully, understand what each award covers and prepare their applications well before the deadlines. A suitable funding plan can help reduce the financial pressure of studying abroad and allow students to focus on their academic goals.
With the right research and preparation, students can explore several ways to make higher education in France more affordable.

living-and-culture.title: Cost of Living in France and French Culture: A Guide for Indian Students
paragraphs: Cost of Living in France and French Culture: A Guide for Indian Students
Introduction

Moving to France for higher education is about more than paying tuition fees and attending classes. You will also be adapting to a new lifestyle, managing everyday expenses, understanding a different culture and building a social life away from home.

France offers a good quality of life, reliable public transport, accessible healthcare arrangements and several student benefits. However, the cost of living can vary considerably depending on where you study. Living in Paris requires a much larger budget than living in cities such as Lille, Grenoble, Toulouse or Montpellier.

For Indian students, it is important to understand both sides of the experience. You should know how much you may spend on accommodation, food, transport and other necessities, but you should also understand what daily life in France looks like.
This guide covers the major living expenses, practical ways to save money and the cultural experiences you can expect as an international student in France.
1. What Is Included in the Cost of Living?
Your cost of living is the amount you spend on everyday necessities and personal activities while studying in France. It is separate from your university tuition fees.
Before travelling, consider the following expenses:

Some of these expenses are fixed every month, while others depend on your lifestyle. Accommodation is usually the biggest expense, so choosing your city and housing arrangement carefully can make a major difference.
2. Average Monthly Cost of Living in France
The amount you need depends on your city, accommodation and spending habits. Paris is generally the most expensive option, while smaller university cities can offer a more manageable lifestyle.

3. Accommodation Costs in France
Accommodation will usually take up the largest part of your monthly budget. France offers several types of student housing, from public university residences to private apartments.
Types of Student Accommodation
1. CROUS Student Residences
CROUS is a public organisation that provides student accommodation and services across France. Its residences are generally among the more affordable housing options.
Approximate rent: €150–€450 per month in many locations.
Rooms and studios are usually furnished.
Some residences include utilities in the rent.
Availability is limited, and applications can be competitive.
CROUS accommodation is particularly useful for students looking to manage their expenses. However, receiving university admission does not automatically guarantee a room.
2. Shared Apartments
Shared accommodation, often called colocation, is a popular option among international students.
Approximate rent: €300–€700 per month outside central Paris.
Rent and some household expenses can be shared.
Students usually have their own bedroom and share common areas.
It can be a good way to meet other students and practise French.
3. Private Studios
Students who prefer privacy can rent a private studio or apartment.
Approximate rent: €500–€1,100 or more, depending on the city.
Offers greater independence.
Usually requires a security deposit and supporting rental documents.
Utilities may be charged separately.
Additional Housing Expenses

Important: Read your rental agreement carefully. Confirm whether electricity, water, heating and internet are included before signing it.
Understanding CAF Housing Assistance
CAF stands for Caisse d'Allocations Familiales. It administers several forms of housing assistance, including APL and ALS, which may help eligible tenants reduce their housing expenses.
However, Indian students need to pay particular attention to the eligibility rules introduced on 1 July 2026.

Most non-EU students holding a residence permit for studies are no longer eligible for housing assistance unless they fall within specified exceptions. These include students receiving an eligible means-tested scholarship or students engaged in professional activity. Certain other categories, such as refugees and stateless persons, are also covered by separate provisions.
If you qualify, the amount depends on your accommodation, rent, income and personal circumstances. There is no guaranteed percentage of rent that will be refunded.
Planning advice: Calculate your budget using the full rent. Treat CAF assistance as an additional benefit only after confirming your eligibility through the official CAF website.
4. Food and Grocery Expenses
France has a strong food culture, with bakeries, cafés, supermarkets and restaurants forming an important part of everyday life.
For Indian students, food expenses will depend on whether they prefer cooking at home, eating at university canteens or visiting restaurants.
Monthly Grocery Budget
A student who mostly cooks at home can plan for approximately €200–€300 per month, depending on the city and food preferences.
Some commonly available supermarket options include:
Lidl: Popular for affordable groceries and household products.
Aldi: Another discount supermarket with budget-friendly options.
E.Leclerc: Offers a wide range of products and competitive prices.
Carrefour: Has both large supermarkets and smaller convenience stores.
Monoprix: Convenient for everyday shopping, but often more expensive.
Indian Food and Grocery Shopping
Students who prefer Indian food can find shops selling rice, lentils, spices, flour and other familiar ingredients in many French cities.
Some areas with Indian and South Asian grocery stores include:
Paris: La Chapelle and the area around Gare du Nord.
Lyon: Guillotière.
Other cities: Look for local international grocery shops and Asian supermarkets.
Cooking familiar meals such as dal, rice, rajma and vegetables can help students manage their food budgets.

The CROUS University Restaurant
One of the most useful student facilities in France is the CROUS university restaurant, commonly called Resto U.

From 4 May 2026, the €1 meal became available to eligible students with an active Izly account at CROUS restaurants. The meal generally includes a main course and up to two additional items, such as a starter, fruit or dessert.
This can make university canteens one of the most affordable ways to eat regularly while studying.
Other Ways to Save on Food
Prepare meals at home instead of ordering food frequently.
Buy groceries in larger supermarkets rather than convenience stores.
Compare prices between different supermarkets.
Use the Too Good To Go app to purchase surplus food from participating businesses.
Look for local markets where seasonal fruits and vegetables may be cheaper.
5. Transportation Costs in France
France has an extensive public transportation network. Most major university cities offer buses, metro systems, trams and regional trains.
Students can usually access discounted transport passes, although the prices and eligibility conditions differ between cities.
Common Modes of Transportation
Metro and Tram: Major cities such as Paris, Lyon, Lille, Marseille and Toulouse have metro or tram networks. These are commonly used for daily travel to universities and workplaces.
Buses: Buses connect residential areas, university campuses and city centres. They are particularly useful in smaller towns.
Regional Trains (TER): TER trains connect nearby towns and cities and are useful for weekend trips.
High-Speed Trains (TGV): TGV trains connect major French cities over longer distances. Booking in advance can help reduce ticket prices.
Bicycle Sharing: Several cities have public bicycle-sharing services. These can be useful for short journeys and daily commuting.

Travelling Between Cities
Students who want to explore France can use:

7. Healthcare and Insurance Expenses
France has a public healthcare system that provides reimbursement for eligible medical expenses.

International students must register with the French social security system through the dedicated student registration process. Registration is free, but it does not mean that every medical expense will be fully reimbursed.
French Social Security
Students can register through the official student portal after arriving and completing the relevant university registration requirements.
The system provides partial reimbursement for eligible medical expenses, such as doctor consultations and certain treatments.
Supplementary Health Insurance
Students may also consider taking out complementary health insurance, commonly called mutuelle.
It can cover some of the costs not reimbursed by the public system. Whether you need it and how much it costs will depend on your healthcare requirements and the policy you select.
Home Insurance
Home insurance is generally required when renting accommodation in France. It protects against certain risks, such as fire and water damage, depending on the policy.
Do not confuse home insurance with health insurance. They cover different needs.

10. Paris vs Other French Cities: Where Should You Live?
Choosing a city is not only an academic decision. It also determines your accommodation costs, transport expenses, lifestyle and access to employment opportunities.
Paris has a strong international environment and a wide range of cultural and professional opportunities. However, students can often manage their expenses more easily in other university cities.
