Why Consider a City Outside Paris?
Lower accommodation costs: Rent can be considerably more affordable in smaller university cities.
Student communities: Cities such as Lille, Toulouse and Montpellier have established student populations and active university communities.
Less expensive daily life: Groceries, transport and leisure activities may cost less depending on the area.
Easy travel: Regional trains and intercity connections make it possible to visit other parts of France without living in the capital.

Paris can still be the right choice if your preferred university or course is located there. The important thing is to compare the full cost of living with the academic and career opportunities available.
11. How Can Indian Students Save Money in France?
Managing your finances becomes easier when you understand the facilities available to students and develop a few practical habits.
1. Apply for Affordable Student Housing
Explore CROUS residences and shared apartments before considering expensive private studios. Start your housing search early because affordable options can be limited.
2. Check CAF Eligibility

If you meet the current eligibility conditions, apply for housing assistance through CAF. Indian students should carefully check the rules introduced in July 2026 before including any housing subsidy in their financial plan.
3. Make Use of CROUS Restaurants
The €1 student meal introduced in May 2026 can help reduce food expenses. Check the participating restaurants and keep your Izly account active.
4. Use Student Transport Passes
Most major cities have discounted transport subscriptions for students or young residents. Compare the available options before buying individual tickets.
5. Use Your Student Identity Card
Your student card can provide discounts at cinemas, theatres, museums, exhibitions and other cultural venues.
6. Buy Second-Hand Items
Students moving out of accommodation often sell furniture, bicycles, books and household equipment. Platforms such as Leboncoin can help you find second-hand products at lower prices.
7. Cook at Home
Preparing meals at home is one of the easiest ways to control food expenses. Indian students can also prepare familiar meals using ingredients from local international grocery stores.
8. Plan Your Travel in Advance
Train fares can vary significantly depending on the date and availability. Booking early and comparing coach services can make weekend travel more affordable.
12. Can International Students Work While Studying in France?
International students holding the appropriate student visa or residence status can generally work part-time alongside their studies.
For most non-EU students, the permitted limit is 964 hours per year, which represents 60% of the normal annual working time.
Common student jobs include:
Retail and supermarket assistants.
Restaurant and café staff.
University campus jobs.
Tutoring and language-related work.
Hospitality and customer service roles.
However, finding a job is not guaranteed. Knowledge of French can improve employment opportunities, especially in customer-facing roles.

Students should also remember that part-time employment is meant to support their studies, not replace the financial resources required for their stay. It is better to arrange sufficient funds before travelling rather than depending on immediate employment after arrival.
Understanding French Culture and Student Life
13. What Is French Culture Like?

France is known for its history, art, architecture, food, fashion, literature and contributions to philosophy and science. However, French culture is not limited to museums and famous landmarks. It is also reflected in everyday routines, social interactions, local traditions and the way people approach food and leisure.
For Indian students, studying in France offers an opportunity to experience a different social environment while becoming familiar with European academic and professional practices.
French culture also varies between regions. Life in Paris is different from life in a coastal town, a university city in the south or a smaller community near the Alps.
14. Language and Communication
French is the official language of France and plays an important role in everyday communication.

Although many universities offer programmes taught in English, students will still encounter French in daily situations such as shopping, travelling, visiting public offices and interacting with local communities.
Learning basic French before arrival can make the transition much easier.
Some useful expressions include:
French Expression
Meaning
Bonjour
Hello / Good morning
Bonsoir
Good evening
Merci
Thank you
S'il vous plaît
Please
Excusez-moi
Excuse me
Au revoir
Goodbye
Parlez-vous anglais ?
Do you speak English?
Je ne comprends pas
I do not understand
Combien ça coûte ?
How much does it cost?
French people generally appreciate it when visitors make an effort to speak their language, even if their French is not perfect.
15. French Food and Eating Habits
Food is an important part of French culture. Meals are often treated as a time to relax, enjoy different flavours and spend time with family or friends.
France is internationally known for its bread, pastries, cheese, wine and regional cuisine.
Popular French Foods
Croissant: A buttery, flaky pastry commonly eaten for breakfast.
Baguette: A long, traditional French bread that is a regular part of everyday meals.
Crêpes: Thin pancakes that can be served with sweet or savoury fillings.
Quiche: A savoury baked dish made with eggs, cream and different fillings.
Ratatouille: A traditional vegetable dish associated with southern France.
Crème brûlée: A dessert made with a creamy custard base and a caramelised sugar topping.
Macarons: Colourful almond-based sweets with different fillings.
What Should Indian Students Expect?

Indian students may initially find the food different from what they are used to at home. However, larger cities have international supermarkets, Indian restaurants and grocery shops where familiar ingredients are available.
Cooking at home can also help students maintain their preferred food habits while controlling their expenses.
16. French Lifestyle and Social Etiquette
Understanding everyday social behaviour can make settling into France easier.
Greetings Matter
A simple Bonjour is commonly used when entering shops, restaurants and other establishments. Greeting people before asking a question is considered polite.
Among friends, people may greet each other with la bise, a cheek-kissing greeting. It is not necessary to initiate this with everyone, especially when meeting someone for the first time.
Punctuality
Arriving on time is generally expected in academic and professional settings. If you are running late for a meeting, inform the other person in advance.
Respect for Personal Space

French people may be more reserved when interacting with strangers. This does not necessarily mean they are unfriendly. Building friendships can take time, and social relationships often develop through repeated interactions.
Dining Etiquette
Meals are often treated as social occasions. People may spend time talking over lunch or dinner instead of finishing their food quickly.
It is also common to wait until everyone has been served before starting a shared meal.
Work-Life Balance

France places importance on personal time, holidays and time away from work. Students may notice that shops, restaurants and public services have different opening hours, particularly on Sundays and public holidays.
17. Festivals and Cultural Celebrations in France
France hosts several national celebrations, music festivals, cultural events and regional traditions throughout the year.
Students can use these occasions to understand French history and become part of local communities.
Festival or Event
When It Takes Place
What It Celebrates
Bastille Day
14 July
French National Day, commemorating the French Revolution
Fête de la Musique
21 June
Music performances across cities and towns
Cannes Film Festival
Usually May
International cinema and filmmaking
Nice Carnival
Usually February or March
One of the major carnival celebrations in France
Festival of Lights, Lyon
December
Artistic light installations across the city
Christmas Markets
November–December
Seasonal markets, food and regional crafts
Bastille Day
Bastille Day is celebrated on 14 July and is one of the most important national holidays in France. Cities organise public celebrations, parades, concerts and fireworks.
Fête de la Musique
Held on 21 June, this music festival brings performances to streets, public squares, parks and other venues. It is a good opportunity for students to experience the local music scene.
Cannes Film Festival
The Cannes Film Festival is one of the world's most recognised film events. It attracts filmmakers, actors, journalists and cinema enthusiasts from different countries.
Festival of Lights in Lyon
Lyon hosts its famous Festival of Lights in December. Buildings, streets and public spaces are decorated with artistic light displays, attracting visitors from across France and abroad.
18. Art, Museums and Architecture

France has a strong connection with art, literature and architecture. Students interested in history, design, fashion, photography or cinema will find many opportunities to explore these subjects outside the classroom.
Some well-known cultural attractions include:
Louvre Museum, Paris: Home to internationally recognised works of art, including the Mona Lisa.
Musée d'Orsay, Paris: Known for its collection of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist art.
Palace of Versailles: A historic royal palace known for its architecture and gardens.
Centre Pompidou, Paris: A major cultural institution associated with modern and contemporary art.
Musée des Confluences, Lyon: A museum exploring science, society and human history.
Student Discounts and Free Entry
Students can access reduced prices at many museums, theatres and cultural venues.

However, free entry rules depend on the institution, age, nationality and residence status. For example, free admission to many French national museums for visitors under 26 generally applies to EU nationals and certain eligible residents, rather than automatically covering every international student.
Always check the official website of the attraction before planning your visit.
19. Regional Differences: Exploring France Beyond Paris
French culture is not the same throughout the country. Different regions have their own food traditions, landscapes, architecture, festivals and ways of life.
Paris and Île-de-France
Paris is the country's political, cultural and economic centre. It offers museums, theatres, historic monuments, fashion districts and a large international population.
Students can explore areas such as Montmartre, the Latin Quarter and the banks of the Seine.
Provence and the French Riviera
The southern region is known for its Mediterranean coastline, warm climate, markets and outdoor lifestyle.
Cities such as Nice, Marseille and Aix-en-Provence offer a different atmosphere from the busy capital.
Lyon and the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes Region

Lyon is famous for its food culture, historic neighbourhoods and riverside setting. The wider region also offers access to the French Alps, making it attractive to students who enjoy outdoor activities.
Toulouse and Occitanie
Toulouse is known as the Pink City because of its distinctive terracotta architecture. It has a lively student environment and strong links with the aerospace industry.
Lille and Northern France
Lille has a strong student population, historic architecture and a cultural influence shaped partly by its proximity to Belgium.
Its location also makes travel to other European destinations convenient.
20. Student Life and Making Friends in France
University life in France offers more than lectures, assignments and examinations. Students can participate in clubs, sports, cultural activities and student-led organisations.
Student Associations
Many universities have student associations that organise events, social gatherings, workshops and cultural activities.
One important type is the BDE (Bureau des Étudiants), which is generally responsible for student activities and social events within an institution or programme.
International student associations can also help newcomers settle in and connect with people from different backgrounds.
Sports and Fitness
Universities and local sports organisations offer opportunities to participate in activities such as football, basketball, swimming, tennis and fitness training.
Some institutions provide sports facilities or discounted memberships for enrolled students.
International Communities
France attracts students from many countries, including India. Larger university cities often have international student groups and cultural communities.
These groups can make it easier to find familiar food, celebrate Indian festivals and meet people who have experienced a similar transition.
Weekend Activities
Students can use weekends to explore their city, visit museums, attend music events, enjoy local markets or travel to nearby towns.
These experiences can help students develop friendships and become more comfortable with their surroundings.
21. Adjusting to Life in France as an Indian Student
Moving from India to France can involve a significant lifestyle change. The language, weather, food habits, academic environment and social routines may feel unfamiliar at first.
A few practical steps can make the transition easier.
Learn basic French: Even a beginner-level understanding can help with shopping, transport and everyday communication.
Build a routine: Plan your meals, classes, grocery shopping and study time to avoid unnecessary expenses and stress.
Stay connected with home: Keep in touch with family and friends while also making an effort to develop a social circle in France.
Explore local communities: Join student associations, attend university events and participate in activities outside your academic programme.
Be open to different experiences: Trying local food, visiting cultural attractions and learning about regional traditions can make your time in France more rewarding.
Understand local rules: Learn about rental agreements, public transport regulations, healthcare procedures and university requirements before you need them.
Adjusting to a new country takes time. It is normal to experience a period of adaptation, especially during the first few months.
22. First-Month Checklist for Students Arriving in France
The first few weeks after arrival are important because several practical tasks need to be completed.
Before Leaving India
Arrange accommodation and keep a copy of your rental agreement.
Prepare sufficient funds for rent, deposits and initial expenses.
Carry your passport, visa, admission letter and other required documents.
Keep digital and physical copies of important paperwork.
Check whether your accommodation includes utilities and home insurance.
Arrange suitable travel insurance for the initial period, if required.
During the First Week
Complete the applicable visa validation or residence formalities.
Obtain a French SIM card or a suitable mobile plan.
Familiarise yourself with the local transport system.
Complete university registration and collect your student card.
Locate the nearest supermarket, pharmacy and university facilities.
Check the process for opening a bank account.
During the First Month
Register for French social security through the official student portal.
Check your eligibility for CAF housing assistance before relying on it.
Activate your Izly account if you plan to use CROUS services.
Explore student associations and university activities.
Prepare a monthly budget based on your actual expenses.
Locate nearby Indian grocery stores if you need familiar ingredients.
Frequently Asked Questions
1. What is the average cost of living in France for Indian students?
A student may need approximately €750–€1,200 per month outside Paris, depending on accommodation and lifestyle. In Paris, a budget of around €1,100–€1,600 or more may be necessary.
2. Is Paris more expensive than other French cities?
Yes. Accommodation is generally more expensive in Paris, and everyday expenses can also be higher. Cities such as Toulouse, Lille, Grenoble and Montpellier can offer more affordable alternatives.
3. Can Indian students receive CAF housing assistance in France?

Eligibility rules changed on 1 July 2026. Most non-EU students holding a study residence permit are no longer eligible unless they meet specified exceptions, such as receiving an eligible means-tested scholarship or engaging in professional activity. Students should confirm their individual eligibility through CAF.
4. How much does food cost for a student in France?
A student who mainly cooks at home may spend around €200–€300 per month on groceries. Eating out regularly can increase this amount.
5. Can international students eat at university canteens?
Yes. CROUS university restaurants serve students at subsidised prices. From May 2026, the €1 meal became available to eligible students with an active Izly account.
6. Can Indian students work part-time in France?
Most non-EU students with the appropriate student residence status can work up to 964 hours per year. Employment is subject to the applicable rules and should not interfere with academic commitments.
7. Is French necessary for studying in France?

Not always. Some universities offer programmes entirely in English. However, learning French is useful for daily communication, making friends, accessing local services and improving employment opportunities.
8. Is France a good place for Indian students who enjoy travelling?
France has a well-developed public transport and railway network. Students can explore different regions through regional trains, high-speed trains, buses and carpooling services.
9. What is French student life like?

Student life includes academic activities, student associations, sports, cultural events, social gatherings and opportunities to explore different cities. The experience varies depending on the university and location.
10. Are museums and cultural attractions free for international students?

Some museums offer student discounts, and certain national museums provide free entry to eligible visitors under 26. However, the rules depend on age, nationality, residence status and the individual institution.
Conclusion
Studying in France offers an opportunity to experience a different education system, develop international exposure and become part of a diverse cultural environment.

The cost of living requires proper planning, particularly when it comes to accommodation and everyday expenses. Students who compare cities, use university facilities and manage their spending can make their experience more financially comfortable.

At the same time, life in France extends beyond the classroom. From its food and festivals to its museums, regional traditions and student communities, the country offers plenty of opportunities to learn and explore.

For Indian students, the key is to arrive prepared, understand the local system and remain open to a new way of life. With the right planning, studying in France can become a valuable academic and personal experience.

study-in-france.title: Study in France: A Complete Guide for Indian Students (2026–27)
paragraphs: Study in France: A Complete Guide for Indian Students (2026–27)

France offers a higher education system that works differently from many other popular study destinations. Its public universities operate alongside selective Grandes Écoles, specialised institutions and internationally recognised business and engineering schools. Combined with government-supported education, English-taught programmes and access to European academic networks, France gives Indian students several routes to an international degree.

What makes France particularly interesting is the range of choices available. You can pursue a traditional university degree, specialise in luxury brand management, study engineering at a dedicated grande école, or explore hospitality, fashion and culinary arts at specialist institutions.

However, choosing France requires understanding its education structure, language expectations, admission procedures, tuition arrangements and residence rules. This guide covers the important details to consider before applying.
1. Why Study in France for Indian Students?

France has developed an international education system that combines academic research, specialised professional training and strong government involvement in higher education. For Indian students, several features make it worth considering.
A distinctive system of Grandes Écoles

One of the most recognisable features of French education is the Grandes Écoles system. These institutions operate alongside traditional universities and offer selective programmes in areas such as business, engineering, public administration and political science.
Many have close connections with employers and professional sectors. Institutions such as HEC Paris and École Polytechnique illustrate the specialised nature of this pathway.
Admission can be competitive, and requirements vary considerably between institutions.
Government support for public higher education

Public universities in France receive substantial government funding, which helps keep tuition comparatively accessible in many cases. International students may encounter differentiated tuition rates, exemptions or institution-specific arrangements, so the fee must be checked for the particular programme and intake.
This makes public universities an important option for students comparing the cost of studying in France with other European destinations.
Strong connections with specialised industries
France has a well-established presence in luxury goods, fashion, hospitality, aerospace, engineering, pharmaceuticals and financial services.
For students interested in these industries, specialised academic programmes can offer exposure to relevant business environments, professional projects and internships, depending on the institution.
English-taught programmes with European exposure

Students can find English-taught programmes in business, management, engineering, technology and other disciplines. This allows international applicants to pursue a degree without necessarily having advanced French proficiency before arrival.
However, learning French remains valuable for everyday communication, internships, professional networking and employment opportunities within the country.
An established academic relationship with India

France and India have expanded their educational cooperation, including an ambition to welcome 30,000 Indian students in France by 2030. This reflects growing academic engagement between the two countries and creates an encouraging environment for students exploring French institutions.
2. Understanding the French Education System

France follows the European Licence-Master-Doctorat (LMD) framework, which organises higher education into three main qualification levels. This structure makes it easier to understand degree progression and compare academic qualifications across participating European countries.
Undergraduate Education: Licence
A Licence is the standard undergraduate qualification in France and generally takes three years to complete.
Duration: 3 years (6 semesters).
Credits: 180 ECTS.
Eligibility: Completion of Class 12 or an equivalent secondary qualification.
Popular fields: Business, economics, computer science, engineering, humanities, law and social sciences.
Students usually begin with foundational subjects before moving towards more specialised areas of their chosen discipline.
Postgraduate Education: Master
A French Master's degree generally takes two years and allows students to develop advanced subject knowledge or specialise in a professional field.
Duration: 2 years (4 semesters).
Credits: 120 ECTS after completing a Licence or equivalent qualification.
Eligibility: A relevant bachelor's degree or equivalent academic qualification.
Popular fields: Management, finance, engineering, data science, luxury brand management and international business.

Some institutions also offer specialised Master's programmes with different admission conditions and structures. Students should distinguish between a nationally recognised Master's degree and other postgraduate qualifications offered by private institutions.
Doctoral Education: Doctorat
The Doctorat is France's highest academic qualification and focuses on original research within a specialised subject.
Duration: Generally 3 years after a Master's degree, although some projects take longer.
Credits: Research-based progression rather than a conventional taught-degree structure.
Eligibility: A relevant Master's qualification and acceptance into an appropriate doctoral research project.
Popular fields: Mathematics, physics, biotechnology, engineering, economics and social sciences.
Doctoral candidates generally work with research supervisors and may receive funding through research contracts, institutional grants or other arrangements.
How ECTS Credits Work
The European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System (ECTS) measures academic workload and supports the comparison and recognition of higher education qualifications across Europe.
Qualification
Typical duration
ECTS credits
Licence
3 years
Master
2 years
120 additional
Doctorat
Usually 3 years
Research-based
The LMD structure is particularly useful for Indian students comparing bachelor's and postgraduate pathways before applying to French institutions.
3. How Teaching and Assessment Work in France
The French academic environment combines structured classroom instruction with independent study and practical academic activities.
Students may encounter several teaching formats:
Cours Magistraux (CM): Large lectures where professors introduce theories, concepts and subject foundations.
Travaux Dirigés (TD): Smaller tutorial sessions involving exercises, discussions and applied learning.
Travaux Pratiques (TP): Practical sessions, particularly in science, engineering and laboratory-based programmes.
Research Projects: Assignments and independent investigations that help students develop subject expertise.
Internships (Stages): Professional placements that may form part of the programme, depending on the institution and qualification.
Assessment methods vary between institutions. Written examinations, presentations, coursework, group projects and research assignments may all contribute to final grades.
Students should also prepare for a relatively high degree of independent learning, particularly at public universities.
4. Intakes and Application Timelines in France
France generally follows an academic calendar beginning around September, although the exact application schedule depends on the institution and programme.
September/October Intake
Main intake
The September or October intake is the primary admission period for French higher education institutions.
Offers the widest range of undergraduate and postgraduate programmes.
Most public universities organise their academic year around this intake.
Many scholarship opportunities follow deadlines several months before classes begin.
Students should ideally begin researching programmes during the preceding academic year.
January/February Intake
Limited availability
The January or February intake is available at selected institutions, particularly in certain business, management and specialised postgraduate programmes.
Programme availability is more limited than the autumn intake.
Some private institutions offer additional admission cycles.
Application deadlines vary considerably.
Scholarship availability may differ from the main intake.

Planning recommendation: Begin your university research and documentation at least 8–12 months before your intended start date. Some scholarship and selective-school applications require even earlier preparation.
5. Popular Courses to Study in France

France offers academic opportunities across traditional university subjects and specialised professional disciplines. Its international reputation in business, luxury goods, engineering, hospitality and scientific research makes it particularly relevant for students exploring specialised degrees.
1. Business and Management

Popular programmes include MBA, Master in Management, International Business, Finance, Marketing and Entrepreneurship. France has a well-established business-school ecosystem with institutions such as HEC Paris, ESSEC and ESCP.
2. Engineering and Technology

Aerospace, mechanical, civil, electrical, automotive and industrial engineering are important study areas. Engineering schools often combine scientific foundations with technical projects and industry-oriented training.
3. Computer Science, AI and Data Science

Students can explore artificial intelligence, machine learning, cybersecurity, software engineering, data analytics and computer science through specialised programmes at French universities and engineering schools.
4. Luxury Brand Management and Fashion
France offers specialised programmes in luxury management, fashion marketing, fashion design, retail strategy and brand communication, supported by its established luxury and fashion industries.
5. Hospitality, Tourism and Culinary Arts

Hotel management, international hospitality, tourism, gastronomy and culinary management are popular choices. Institutions such as Le Cordon Bleu and Ferrandi Paris offer specialised professional training.
6. Healthcare and Life Sciences

Biotechnology, pharmaceutical sciences, public health, biomedical research and healthcare management provide options for students interested in scientific and healthcare-related careers. Clinical programmes may have additional language and professional recognition requirements.
7. Architecture and Interior Design
Architecture, urban planning, interior design and sustainable building programmes combine creative development with technical and spatial knowledge.
8. Economics, Finance and International Relations
Programmes in economics, banking, investment, international development, public policy and political science provide pathways into financial institutions, research and international organisations.
Choosing the Right Course
Before selecting a programme, compare:
Whether the qualification is nationally recognised or institution-specific.
The language in which lectures and assessments are conducted.
Internship opportunities and industry partnerships.
Admission requirements and academic prerequisites.
Tuition fees and available scholarships.
Career opportunities in France and other countries.
A specialised course should be selected for its academic quality and relevance, not simply because it carries a popular subject title.
6. Types of Universities and Institutions in France
Understanding the different institution types is essential because French higher education is not limited to conventional public universities.
Public Universities
Public universities are government-supported institutions offering degrees across a broad range of academic disciplines.
They are particularly relevant for students interested in economics, science, humanities, law, management and research.
Examples include Sorbonne University, Université Paris-Saclay and Université de Lyon.
Grandes Écoles
Grandes Écoles are selective higher education institutions that provide specialised education in areas such as engineering, business, management and public administration.
Their admission processes may involve competitive examinations, academic assessments or separate application procedures.
Examples include HEC Paris, ESSEC Business School, ESCP Business School and École Polytechnique.
Engineering Schools
French engineering schools offer specialised technical education in areas including aerospace, electronics, mechanical engineering, computer science and industrial technology.
Some programmes lead to the Diplôme d'Ingénieur, a nationally recognised engineering qualification accredited through the Commission des Titres d'Ingénieur (CTI).
Private Business and Management Schools
France has a substantial network of private business schools offering undergraduate and postgraduate programmes in management, finance, marketing and international business.
Students should verify the accreditation and recognition of the specific qualification rather than relying exclusively on the institution's reputation.
Specialised Institutions
These institutions focus on particular professional or creative disciplines, including fashion, design, hospitality, culinary arts and architecture.
Examples include Institut Français de la Mode, Le Cordon Bleu and Ferrandi Paris.
7. Top Universities in France
France has a wide network of public universities, engineering schools and specialised higher education institutions. The following institutions are worth exploring when comparing academic options.
Université PSL – Sciences, humanities, economics and research.
Institut Polytechnique de Paris – Engineering, mathematics, technology and applied sciences.
Sorbonne University – Science, medicine, humanities and research.
Université Paris-Saclay – Mathematics, physics, engineering and life sciences.
Université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne – Economics, law, management and humanities.
Université Grenoble Alpes – Engineering, science and technology.
Université de Strasbourg – Medicine, chemistry, science and international studies.
Aix-Marseille Université – Health sciences, law, economics and research.
Université de Bordeaux – Science, medicine, engineering and business.
Université de Montpellier – Life sciences, medicine and environmental studies.
HEC Paris – Business, management, finance and entrepreneurship.
ESSEC Business School – Management, finance and international business.
ESCP Business School – Business, marketing and management.
École Polytechnique – Engineering, mathematics and advanced research.
INSA Lyon – Engineering, technology and applied sciences.

Note: This is a selection of institutions across different academic categories, not a ranking. Check the exact programme, degree recognition, teaching language and admission requirements before applying.
8. English-Taught Programmes and French Language Requirements
One of the important considerations for Indian students is the language of instruction.

France offers a growing selection of programmes taught in English, particularly at Master's level. However, the availability of English-taught bachelor's programmes varies considerably by subject and institution.
Can You Study in France Without Knowing French?
Yes. Students can apply for eligible English-taught programmes without necessarily having prior French-language proficiency.
Depending on the institution, applicants may be asked to demonstrate English proficiency through:
IELTS Academic
TOEFL iBT
PTE Academic
Other accepted English-language qualifications
Previous education in English, where an institution permits an exemption
The required score depends on the university and programme.
Why Learning French Still Matters
Even if your degree is taught in English, French can make a significant difference to your experience.
It helps with:
Everyday communication and social interaction.
Finding internships and professional opportunities.
Understanding local workplace practices.
Networking with French-speaking employers.
Exploring career opportunities beyond English-speaking environments.
For programmes taught in French, applicants may need qualifications such as DELF, DALF or TCF, depending on the institution.

Our recommendation: Choose your programme based on academic suitability first, but consider learning French before departure. It can make your transition into French society and professional life considerably easier.
9. Admission Requirements for Indian Students

Admission requirements in France depend on the degree level, institution and selected programme. Public universities, Grandes Écoles and private institutions may follow different selection procedures.
Bachelor's Admission Requirements
Indian students applying for undergraduate programmes generally need:
Class 12 certificate from a recognised board.
Academic transcripts and mark sheets.
Passport and identity documents.
Statement of purpose or motivation letter, where required.
English or French language proficiency, depending on the programme.
Additional entrance examinations or interviews, where applicable.
Some programmes may have subject prerequisites, particularly in mathematics, science and technical disciplines.
Master's Admission Requirements
For postgraduate programmes, applicants generally need:
A recognised bachelor's degree.
Academic transcripts and graduation certificate.
Updated CV or résumé.
Statement of purpose or motivation letter.
Letters of recommendation, where requested.
English or French proficiency evidence.
Portfolio, entrance test or interview for selected programmes.
Students should pay particular attention to whether their previous bachelor's degree meets the academic prerequisites of the chosen Master's programme.
PhD Admission Requirements
Doctoral applications generally require:
A relevant Master's degree or equivalent.
Research proposal.
Academic transcripts.
Research experience or previous publications, where applicable.
Acceptance or supervision from an appropriate research team.
Evidence of funding or a suitable doctoral funding arrangement, depending on the position.
10. French Student Visa for Indian Students
Indian citizens planning to pursue a full-time degree in France generally require the appropriate long-stay student visa.
The exact visa category depends on the duration and nature of the course.
Long-Stay Student Visa (VLS-TS)
The VLS-TS, or Visa de Long Séjour valant Titre de Séjour, is a long-stay visa that also serves as a residence permit once properly validated.
It is commonly used by international students enrolled in qualifying programmes lasting more than six months.
After arriving in France, students holding a VLS-TS must complete the online validation process within three months.
France-Visas+1
Documents Commonly Required
The application may require:
Valid passport.
University admission or enrolment confirmation.
Campus France documentation, where applicable.
Proof of accommodation or temporary address.
Evidence of sufficient financial resources.
Academic documents.
Passport-sized photographs.
Visa application form and supporting documentation.
Additional documents requested by the consular authorities.
The exact checklist should always be confirmed through France-Visas.
Financial Requirements
Students must demonstrate that they have sufficient financial resources to support their stay in France.

The required amount and acceptable evidence should be checked against the current official visa guidance. Do not rely on an old financial threshold or assume that a university admission letter alone satisfies the requirement.
Schengen Travel
A valid French long-stay visa or residence permit may allow travel within the Schengen Area for short stays, subject to the applicable conditions.
This does not provide an unrestricted right to work or settle in other European countries.
15. Working While Studying in France
International students holding an eligible French student residence status can generally work part-time while pursuing their education.
The standard allowance for most foreign students is up to 964 hours per year, equivalent to approximately 60% of normal annual working hours in France.
France-Visas+1
Where Can Students Work?
Depending on their language skills and experience, students may explore:
Retail and customer service.
Restaurants and hospitality.
University-based student jobs.
Administrative support.
Internships and professional placements.
Part-time roles related to their academic discipline.
Can Part-Time Work Cover Your Expenses?
Part-time employment can help manage daily expenses, but students should not depend on it to finance their entire education.
Work availability, language requirements, academic workload and local employment conditions all influence the income a student can earn.
It is important to arrange sufficient funding before travelling to France.
18. Career Opportunities After Studying in France
France has established professional sectors across business, technology, aerospace, luxury goods, hospitality, pharmaceuticals and research.
Graduates may explore opportunities depending on their qualifications, experience, language proficiency and employment authorisation.
Industry
Potential career areas
Business and Finance
Financial analysis, consulting, management and banking
Engineering
Aerospace, automotive, industrial and mechanical engineering
Technology
Software development, AI, data science and cybersecurity
Luxury and Fashion
Brand management, merchandising and marketing
Hospitality
Hotel operations, tourism and culinary management
Life Sciences
Biotechnology, pharmaceutical research and laboratory work
The Importance of French in Employment
English may be sufficient for certain international companies and specialised positions, but French remains important across much of the domestic employment market.
Students who develop professional French communication skills may have access to a wider range of opportunities.
Build Professional Experience During Your Studies
Students should consider internships, university projects, networking events and relevant part-time employment to develop practical experience.
Some programmes include compulsory internships, while others provide opportunities through institutional or industry partnerships.
11. Is France the Right Study Destination for You?
France can be a suitable destination for students who want a European degree, access to specialised academic institutions and opportunities to study in internationally recognised professional fields.
However, it is important to assess both its advantages and practical considerations.
France may suit you if...
Consider carefully if...
You want access to government-supported public universities.
You are relying on a low tuition estimate without checking exemptions.
You are interested in business, luxury, fashion or engineering.
You expect every programme to be available in English.
You want to study within the European academic framework.
You are unfamiliar with the Campus France application process.
You are interested in research and specialised institutions.
You have not planned your accommodation and living expenses.
You are willing to learn French.
You expect part-time work to finance your complete education.
You want to explore professional opportunities in France.
You are treating post-study residence as a guaranteed route to employment.
Final Considerations

France is not simply a destination for students looking for affordable European education. Its academic system offers different types of institutions, specialised qualifications and professional learning environments that require careful comparison.
For Indian students, the most important step is to identify a recognised programme that matches their academic background, language abilities, budget and career direction.

cost-of-studying.title: Cost of Studying in France for Indian Students
paragraphs: Cost of Studying in France for Indian Students
Introduction

France is an attractive destination for international students because it offers a wide range of academic programmes, internationally recognised qualifications and several affordable public higher education options. However, the cost of studying in France depends heavily on the type of institution, course, degree level and fee policy applicable to international students.

Public universities generally have lower tuition fees because the French government subsidises a significant part of higher education costs. Private universities, business schools and specialised institutions usually charge considerably more. Students also need to account for registration charges, student contributions, application expenses and course-related materials.

For Indian students planning to study in France in 2026–27, understanding these expenses in advance can help them compare universities, prepare a realistic education budget and avoid unexpected payments during the admission process.
This guide focuses on tuition fees and other academic expenses. Accommodation, food, transport and other personal living costs are separate and should be planned independently.
1. What Is Included in the Cost of Studying in France?
The cost of studying in France is not limited to the tuition fee mentioned on a university's website. Students may have to pay several additional charges before and after receiving admission.
The main academic and administrative expenses include:
Tuition Fees: This is the primary expense and covers the academic programme. The amount depends on the university, course, degree level and whether the institution is public or private.

Student and Campus Life Contribution (CVEC): This is an annual contribution used to support student services, healthcare initiatives, cultural activities and campus facilities. The CVEC for the 2026–27 academic year is €105.
Études en France (EEF) Processing Fee: Indian students applying through the Campus France India procedure must account for the EEF processing fee. From 1 August 2026, the fee is ₹20,000.

Student Visa Fee: Indian students applying through the Études en France procedure are generally charged a reduced long-stay student visa fee of €50. The standard fee for other applicants is €99, subject to the applicable visa category and individual circumstances.

VFS Service Charges: Students submitting their visa applications through VFS Global may have to pay a separate service fee. The amount should be checked on the official appointment portal because it can change.

Study Materials and Course Expenses: Depending on the programme, students may need to purchase textbooks, software licences, laboratory equipment, art supplies, design materials or other specialised resources.
These expenses should be considered separately from the main tuition fee when preparing an academic budget.
2. Tuition Fees in France for International Students

Tuition fees in France vary considerably between public universities and private institutions. The French government subsidises public higher education, which allows many students to access degree programmes at a lower cost than they might find in other popular study destinations.
However, Indian students should understand the difference between the standard public university fee and the differentiated tuition fee applicable to many non-EU students.
Undergraduate Tuition Fees
Undergraduate programmes in France are generally offered as Bachelor's degrees, commonly known as Licence programmes.
For the 2026–27 academic year, the standard differentiated tuition fee for non-EU students at public institutions under the French Ministry of Higher Education is €2,902 per year.
Private universities and specialised institutions set their own fees. Depending on the course and institution, annual tuition can range from approximately €5,000 to €15,000 or more.
Postgraduate Tuition Fees
Students applying for a Master's degree should expect different fee structures depending on the institution and programme.
For 2026–27, the standard differentiated tuition fee for non-EU students pursuing a Master's degree at eligible public institutions is €3,950 per year.
Private business schools, management institutes and specialised postgraduate institutions may charge considerably higher fees. Some programmes can cost €8,000 to €30,000 or more annually.
MBA Programme Fees
France is home to several internationally recognised business schools offering MBA and executive management programmes.
MBA fees are usually higher than those of regular public university Master's programmes. The total cost depends on the school's reputation, programme duration, specialisation and additional services.
At leading business schools, the complete programme fee can range from approximately €20,000 to more than €100,000.
Students should check whether the quoted amount covers only tuition or also includes registration, course materials, international modules and other programme-related expenses.
Doctoral and PhD Tuition Fees
Doctoral programmes at public higher education institutions are generally more affordable than undergraduate and Master's programmes.
For 2026–27, the standard doctoral registration fee is €398 per year. Unlike Bachelor's and Master's programmes, PhD studies are not subject to the differentiated non-EU tuition fee.

Some private institutions and specialised professional doctoral programmes may charge higher fees. Students should also check whether their doctoral position is funded through a research contract, university funding or another arrangement.

3. Cost of Specialised Courses in France

France offers academic programmes across engineering, medicine, architecture, business, law, fashion, design and other specialised fields. The tuition structure for these programmes can differ from the standard public university fee.
Some programmes are offered through public universities, while others are delivered by specialised schools and Grandes Écoles. These institutions may have independent fee structures.
1. Engineering Degrees
France has a strong engineering education system, with programmes in aerospace, robotics, energy, computer science, mechanical engineering and other technical fields.
Engineering education is available through public engineering institutions as well as specialised and private schools.

Public Engineering Institutions: Fees depend on the institution and the type of engineering qualification. Some programmes benefit from government-supported fee structures, while others charge separate engineering registration fees.
Grandes Écoles: Prestigious engineering schools may charge higher tuition, particularly for specialised and international programmes.
Private Engineering Schools: Annual tuition can range from approximately €8,000 to €15,000 or more, depending on the institution and specialisation.
Students should not assume that every public engineering school follows the standard Bachelor's or Master's fee structure. The institution's official fee schedule should always be checked.
2. Medical Studies and Healthcare Programmes
Medical education in France follows a structured university-based system. Admission is competitive, and students should understand the academic pathway before applying.
Medical studies are primarily offered through public universities, where tuition and registration charges depend on the programme and the student's fee category.
Public Medical Universities: Fees are determined by the applicable national registration rules and the institution's programme structure.
Private Healthcare Institutions: Specialised private healthcare and related programmes may charge substantially higher fees.
Additional Expenses: Laboratory work, clinical training materials, insurance requirements and other programme-specific costs may add to the overall academic budget.

Indian students interested in medicine should carefully check the language of instruction, admission requirements, duration and professional recognition of the qualification. A medical programme in France should not be compared directly with a conventional MBBS programme in India without understanding the differences in the education systems.
3. Architecture and Urban Planning
France has specialised institutions dedicated to architecture, urban planning and related fields. These include National Schools of Architecture, commonly known as ENSA.
Public Architecture Schools: Fees are generally lower than those of private architecture institutions, but the exact amount depends on the school and applicable fee category.
Private Architecture Schools: Annual tuition may range from approximately €8,000 to €10,500 or more.
Additional Costs: Students may need to purchase drawing materials, model-making supplies, printing services, specialist software and other studio resources.
Architecture students should include these additional expenses when comparing programmes.
4. Art, Design and Fashion
France is an important destination for students interested in fashion, visual arts, graphic design, luxury management and creative industries.
These programmes are offered by public art schools, private design institutes and specialised fashion schools.
Public Fine Arts Institutions: Some public schools offer comparatively affordable tuition, depending on the institution and fee category.
Private Fashion and Design Schools: Annual fees can range from approximately €9,000 to €15,000 or more.
Studio and Material Expenses: Students may need to budget for fabrics, design tools, equipment, software, printing and project materials.
The total cost can vary significantly depending on the practical requirements of the course.
5. Law and Legal Studies
French universities offer undergraduate and postgraduate programmes in law, international law, European law and related disciplines.
Public Universities: Students generally pay the applicable national registration fee, depending on their degree level and fee category.
Specialised LL.M Programmes: International and professionally focused law programmes may charge higher fees, particularly when offered by specialised institutions or business schools.
Additional Expenses: Students may need to purchase legal textbooks, academic publications and other course materials.
Applicants should also consider the language of instruction. Many French law programmes require strong French-language ability, while selected international law programmes are offered in English.

4. Public Universities vs Private Universities in France
One of the most important decisions affecting the cost of studying in France is the choice between a public university and a private institution.
Both offer different academic experiences, course options and fee structures.
Public Universities
Public universities receive substantial financial support from the French government. This helps keep tuition fees relatively affordable compared with many private institutions.
For international students, however, differentiated tuition fees may apply to certain Bachelor's and Master's programmes.
Public universities can be a suitable option for students who want to manage their academic expenses while pursuing recognised degrees.
Private Universities and Grandes Écoles

Private institutions and Grandes Écoles generally have independent fee structures. Their programmes may focus on specialised areas such as business management, engineering, luxury management, fashion, hospitality and international relations.
Some institutions offer industry-focused teaching, professional projects, internships and specialised facilities. These features may contribute to higher programme fees.

However, a higher tuition fee does not automatically mean a better academic outcome. Students should compare course content, accreditation, faculty, industry links, graduate outcomes and total programme costs before making a decision.

5. Additional Academic and Application Expenses
Tuition is usually the largest academic expense, but students should also prepare for smaller payments that arise during the admission and enrolment process.
1. CVEC Fee
The Student and Campus Life Contribution, known as CVEC, is an annual payment for many students enrolling in French higher education institutions.
For the 2026–27 academic year, the contribution is €105.
It supports student services and campus initiatives, including healthcare access, cultural activities, sports and social support.
Some categories of students are exempt. Students should check their eligibility and obtain the relevant payment or exemption certificate before completing university registration.
2. Études en France Processing Fee
Indian students applying through the Campus France India Études en France procedure must pay the applicable processing fee.
From 1 August 2026, the EEF fee is ₹20,000.

The payment is made after the application file has been validated and the official payment link has been issued. Students should follow the instructions on the official Campus France platform rather than making payments through unofficial links.
3. Student Visa Fee
Students pursuing a course lasting more than three months generally require a long-stay student visa.
For applicants covered by the Études en France procedure, the indicative visa fee is €50. The standard long-stay visa fee for other applicants is €99.
The final amount depends on the applicable visa category and circumstances. Students should confirm the fee through France-Visas before submitting their application.
4. VFS Service Charges
VFS Global handles the submission process for visa applications in India on behalf of the French authorities.
A separate service charge may apply. Optional services, such as courier delivery and SMS notifications, can increase the amount paid.
Students should check the latest charges on the official VFS appointment portal.
5. University Application and Registration Charges
Some institutions may charge application, entrance examination or administrative fees.
These charges are not the same across all universities. Students should check the admission page and fee schedule of each institution before submitting an application.
6. Entrance Examination Fees
Depending on the programme, students may need to take standardised tests or institution-specific entrance examinations.
Possible expenses include:
IELTS or TOEFL, where required by the institution.
GMAT or GRE, where required for selected postgraduate programmes.
Institution-specific entrance examinations.
Portfolio preparation or assessment charges for creative programmes.
Not every student needs to take these examinations. The requirement depends on the university and course.
7. Study Materials and Specialised Equipment
Certain academic programmes involve practical work and additional learning resources.
Examples include:
Textbooks and academic publications.
Laboratory equipment and protective materials.
Architecture and model-making supplies.
Art, fashion and design materials.
Computer software and technical tools.
Printing, studio and project expenses.
These costs should be checked with the department or programme coordinator because they can differ considerably between courses.
8. Initial Tuition Deposits
Some private institutions require students to pay an initial deposit after receiving an admission offer.
This payment may secure the student's place in the programme and can later be adjusted against tuition fees, depending on the institution's refund and payment policy.
Students should carefully read the payment terms before transferring any deposit, particularly the conditions applicable if a visa is refused or the student decides not to enrol.

7. Scholarships That Can Reduce the Cost of Studying in France

Students do not always have to fund the entire cost of their education independently. Several French government, institutional and international scholarship programmes provide financial assistance to eligible students.
Scholarships may cover tuition, provide a monthly allowance or support selected academic and living expenses. Their benefits differ, so students should read the conditions carefully.
1. France Excellence Eiffel Scholarship
The Eiffel Excellence Scholarship is a French government scholarship designed to attract high-achieving international students to Master's and doctoral programmes.
It provides financial support and additional services to selected candidates.
For 2026, the monthly allowance is:
Master's level: €1,200 per month.
Doctoral level: €2,000 per month.
The programme may also provide support for international and domestic transportation, insurance, accommodation searches and cultural activities.
Important: The Eiffel scholarship does not directly pay tuition fees. Students should confirm the tuition arrangements with the institution nominating them for the scholarship.

Applications are submitted by French higher education institutions on behalf of candidates. Students should therefore contact their chosen institution to understand its selection process and deadlines.
2. France Excellence Charpak Scholarship
The Charpak scholarship programme is designed specifically for Indian students pursuing selected study opportunities in France.
Different Charpak categories support different academic pathways, including Bachelor's studies, Master's studies and exchange programmes.
The Charpak Master's scholarship provides selected students with:
A monthly living allowance of €860.
Exemption from the applicable student visa fee when applying from India.
Exemption from Campus France procedure fees.
Student social security and additional health insurance.
Assistance in finding affordable student accommodation, subject to availability.
Access to discounted university meals and selected student activities.
The scholarship does not cover international travel from India to France or every expense associated with the student's stay.
Eligibility conditions, age limits, academic requirements and application deadlines vary by scholarship category. Students should check the relevant Charpak announcement before applying.
3. Erasmus+
Erasmus+ supports international education and academic mobility through participating institutions and approved programmes.
Eligible students may receive financial support for an exchange period or selected joint Master's programmes involving European institutions.
The availability and amount of funding depend on the programme, participating universities and scholarship conditions.
4. University-Specific Scholarships
Several French universities and private institutions provide their own scholarships and financial assistance.
These awards may be based on academic performance, financial need, nationality, course selection or other eligibility requirements.
Examples include:
Émile Boutmy Scholarship at Sciences Po.
Scholarships and financial assistance offered by Université Paris-Saclay.
Merit-based awards offered by selected business schools.
Department-specific and international student scholarships.
Students should check each university's official scholarship page to understand the application process, award value and renewal requirements.
8. How Scholarships Affect Your Academic Budget
A scholarship can reduce the amount a student needs to arrange independently, but the financial benefit depends on what the award actually covers.
For example, a scholarship may provide a monthly allowance without paying the university's tuition fee. Another award may offer a tuition reduction but no monthly financial support.
Before accepting a scholarship, students should check:
Whether the scholarship covers full or partial tuition.
Whether it provides a monthly allowance.
Whether the award includes health insurance.
Whether visa or application fees are covered.
Whether the scholarship is renewable every academic year.
Whether students must maintain a minimum academic performance.
Whether travel, accommodation deposits and other expenses are excluded.
A scholarship should be evaluated according to its complete financial coverage rather than its advertised award amount alone.
9. Is Studying in France Worth the Investment?
The financial value of studying in France depends on the student's academic goals, chosen institution, programme costs and career plans.

For students selecting affordable public university programmes, France can offer access to recognised higher education at a comparatively manageable tuition cost. Specialised private programmes may require a much larger investment, so their value should be assessed carefully.
A few factors are worth considering before making a decision.
International Academic Recognition
French higher education institutions offer programmes across a wide range of disciplines. A degree from a recognised institution can support opportunities in France and other international markets.
Students should check the institution's accreditation, degree recognition and professional requirements relevant to their intended career.
Industry Exposure
France has established industries in areas such as aerospace, engineering, luxury goods, fashion, hospitality, finance and technology.
Depending on the programme, students may have access to internships, industry projects, professional networks and university career services.
Part-Time Work Opportunities
International students holding the relevant student status can generally work up to 964 hours per year, equivalent to 60% of the normal annual working time in France.
However, part-time work should be treated as supplementary income. It should not be considered a guaranteed way to pay the full tuition fee or cover all personal expenses.
Post-Study Opportunities
Eligible international graduates of certain French higher education programmes may apply for a temporary residence permit to look for employment or establish a business.
The job-search or business-creation residence permit has specific qualification and eligibility conditions. It is not automatically granted to every international graduate.
Students should verify the current rules before using post-study employment opportunities as part of their financial planning.
10. How to Plan Your Study Budget for France
A clear financial plan can help students compare universities and understand how much funding they need before beginning the application process.
The following steps can make the process easier.
Step 1: Select Your Course and Degree Level
Start by identifying the course you want to pursue and whether you are applying for a Bachelor's, Master's, MBA or doctoral programme.
Step 2: Compare Public and Private Institutions
Shortlist universities according to their course offerings, academic reputation, location and tuition fee structure.
Step 3: Confirm the Applicable Tuition Fee
Do not rely only on general fee estimates. Ask the institution whether the standard national fee, differentiated non-EU fee or a separate programme fee applies to you.
Step 4: Check Additional Academic Charges
Include the CVEC, application fees, registration charges, deposits, examination expenses and course materials in your calculations.
Step 5: Explore Scholarship Opportunities
Check government scholarships, Charpak awards, Erasmus+ opportunities and university-specific funding before finalising your budget.
Step 6: Prepare Your Visa and Application Budget
Account for the Études en France processing fee, student visa fee and applicable VFS charges.
Step 7: Calculate the Complete Programme Cost
If your programme lasts two years or more, calculate the tuition and academic expenses for the entire duration rather than looking at only the first-year fee.

Frequently Asked Questions
1. How much does it cost to study in France for Indian students?

For 2026–27, the standard differentiated tuition fee at eligible public institutions is €2,902 per year for Bachelor's programmes and €3,950 per year for Master's programmes. Private institutions and specialised schools set their own fees, which can be considerably higher.
2. Are public universities in France free for international students?

No. Public universities receive government funding, but many non-EU students are required to pay differentiated tuition fees. Some students may qualify for exemptions or reduced fees depending on their circumstances and the institution's policy.
3. What is the tuition fee for a Master's degree in France?
The standard differentiated tuition fee for non-EU students at eligible public institutions is €3,950 per year for 2026–27. Private universities and specialised business schools may charge more.
4. What is the CVEC fee in France?

The CVEC is the Student and Campus Life Contribution. It is €105 for the 2026–27 academic year and supports student services, healthcare initiatives, campus activities and social programmes. Certain categories of students are exempt.
5. How much is the Campus France fee for Indian students?
The Études en France processing fee in India is ₹20,000 from 1 August 2026. Students should pay only after receiving the official payment instructions following validation of their application file.
6. Does the France student visa fee include VFS charges?
No. The visa processing fee and VFS service charges are separate. The applicable VFS fee and any optional services should be checked through the official appointment portal.
7. Can Indian students get scholarships to study in France?

Yes. Indian students can explore opportunities such as the France Excellence Charpak Scholarship, France Excellence Eiffel Scholarship, Erasmus+ funding and university-specific scholarships. Eligibility and benefits vary by programme.
8. Does the Eiffel Scholarship cover tuition fees?

No. The France Excellence Eiffel Scholarship provides a monthly allowance and additional support, but it does not directly cover tuition fees. Students should confirm the tuition arrangements with the institution.
9. Is France affordable for Indian students?

France can be an affordable option for students who secure admission to public universities with manageable tuition fees. However, private business schools and specialised institutions can require a significantly higher academic budget.
10. Are living expenses included in the tuition fees?
No. Tuition fees cover academic instruction and the applicable registration charges. Accommodation, food, transport, personal expenses and other living costs must be budgeted separately.
Conclusion

The cost of studying in France depends largely on the university, course and fee category applicable to the student. Public universities can offer comparatively affordable academic options, while private institutions and specialised schools may require a larger investment.

For Indian students, the most important step is to understand the complete fee structure before accepting an offer. Tuition, registration charges, CVEC, application expenses and course-specific costs should all be considered when preparing an education budget.
With careful university selection, scholarship research and financial planning, students can make a more informed decision about pursuing higher education in France.
